summary:
South Chungcheong Province stands under South Korea's national framework. South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available and the requirement of surgery is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that forcing surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change their gender in the family relations register. Trans visitors have a documented, judicially enforced right to public restrooms: on 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court issued a final, unappealed ruling that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won in compensation against the state.

Nationally there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on these grounds. In healthcare, the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner; the Constitutional Court did issue a landmark 2024 ruling extending same-sex partners a measure of recognition in healthcare.

The province's own record concerns a student human-rights ordinance in force since 10 July 2020 whose Article 15 stipulates non-discrimination obligations based on gender identity and sexual orientation. That obligation runs to enrolled students and school staff rather than to visitors, so it does not govern what a trans traveller faces on the ground. No traveller-facing enforcement action, arrest or event obstruction is documented for this unit.

The ordinance nonetheless remains in effect after a repeal fight: the Chungcheongnam-do provincial council passed a repeal bill on 24 April 2024, the Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education challenged it before the Supreme Court on 13 May 2024 and obtained suspension of the repeal's execution on 30 May 2024, and the Office of Education argues the repeal violates the Constitution and international human-rights treaties. Read as a signal, the province carries a hostile council initiative alongside a protective institutional response, in a national context where Human Rights Watch records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report alongside a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society, and where organised conservative opposition is active. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.
tangentialFactors:
The student human-rights framework adopted in South Chungcheong is a national pattern rather than a local novelty: English Wikipedia lists Chungcheongnam-do among the jurisdictions that enacted such an ordinance, in 2020, and records the same 2024 repeal vote, with the framework's provisions on gender and sexual diversity named the most contentious items. The framework prohibits discrimination of students by gender, religion, nationality, disability, race and sexual orientation.

The repeal litigation is not confined to this province. The Republic of Korea's 21 February 2025 response to the Joint Communication from UN Special Procedures (ref. OL KOR 3/2024) also records the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education's 11 July 2024 petition against its council's abolition and the Supreme Court's 23 July 2024 suspension, with both offices of education filed as 'stakeholders (enforcing authorities)'. Parallel challenges in two provinces indicate coordinated institutional resistance to repeal rather than an isolated local outcome.

The surrounding national context continues to bear on a visitor's assessment: organised conservative opposition to LGBT recognition is active, no national anti-discrimination law exists, and Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report documents persistent discrimination against LGBT people while rating the country's overall record for free media and civil society relatively positively.
localsOnly:
The Chungcheongnam-do student human-rights ordinance, in force from 10 July 2020, imposes non-discrimination obligations on schools covering gender identity and sexual orientation through its Article 15. Its benefits and duties attach to enrolled students and school staff, and the Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education acts as the enforcing authority in the repeal dispute.

For residents, the operative question is whether the repeal takes effect. The provincial council's repeal bill of 24 April 2024 was challenged by the Office of Education on 13 May 2024 and suspended by the Supreme Court on 30 May 2024, so the ordinance continues to bind schools while the litigation is pending. The Office of Education maintains that the repeal violates the Constitution and international human-rights treaties.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources disagree on the ordinance's current status and the discrepancy is unresolved here. The Republic of Korea's 21 February 2025 response to UN Special Procedures states that the Supreme Court suspended execution of the repeal on 30 May 2024 and that the ordinance remains in effect, while the English Wikipedia article on ordinances of student rights records the Chungcheongnam-do ordinance as 'revoked in 2024'. The present record follows the government filing, which is the more recent and more specific account, but the Wikipedia wording has not been reconciled with it.

Not sourced: whether any provision of the ordinance has ever been invoked on behalf of a transgender student in this province, and whether the suspension will hold after final judgment. Whether the province's ordinance protections extend to visitors or non-students is not addressed in the inventory, and no evidence of school-level enforcement practice is available here.
